scenes.name: The Rolling Stones
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Andrew Loog Oldham, su Svengali adolescente, los moldeó como los anti-Beatles: groseros y divisivos, «monstruos melenudos del Id adolescente» (tras la multa por orinar contra el muro de un garaje en 1965, puso a Jagger en el titular). En 1965 «(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction», con su fuzz y su racimo final de «no», expresó una insatisfacción casi cósmica con el consumismo que los había encumbrado; Jagger, culto y elocuente en Charlie Is My Darling de Peter Whitehead, decía que el pop por fin hablaba de levantarse, ir a trabajar y sentirse jodido. «19th Nervous Breakdown» (4 de febrero de 1966), grabado en Los Ángeles al final de una gira de cuarenta fechas, fue la primera gran declaración pop del año: dos guitarras metálicas entrelazadas (Richards y Brian Jones por última vez en un single), ritmo rockabilly maníaco, casi cuatro minutos sobre una pobre niña rica sin salida. Cada single debía superar al anterior en doce semanas. Mientras se codeaban con Anita Pallenberg, Robert Fraser o Christopher Gibbs, Aftermath (abril), entero de composiciones propias, fue el LP del año, aunque en «Stupid Girl» o «Under My Thumb» el desprecio por las mujeres no inquietó a nadie.

scenes.name: La India en el pop: sitar y raga rock
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: La música india se convirtió en la metáfora sonora central del LSD: el dron del sitar y la longitud de las piezas reproducían la dislocación del tiempo, el timbre vibraba en el cuerpo, había un impulso religioso y, a oídos occidentales, ni ego ni formato de tres minutos. Entró en el pop con «See My Friends» de los Kinks, «Heart Full of Soul» de los Yardbirds y la banda sonora de Help!, donde los Beatles descubrieron el sitar poco después de su primer ácido. Jim Dickson, mánager de los Byrds, tenía relación con World Pacific, que grababa a Ravi Shankar (Portrait of a Genius, Sound of the Sitar); Tony Hall recomendaba vivir con sus discos y Harrison quedó deslumbrado al verlo en el Festival Hall. En 1966 llegaron «Eight Miles High», «Shapes of Things», «Paint It, Black» y «Tomorrow Never Knows».

podcast.title: Murder Theories and Unclosed Investigation
podcast.body: Many have questioned the official cause of Brian Jones's death. A prominent theory suggests he was killed by Frank Thorogood, a construction worker on Jones's property and the last person to see him alive. Speculation includes a fight over money, a confession by Thorogood to a friend, and police bungling the investigation. Despite the case being officially closed, Jones's children continue to believe their father was murdered. "The first theory is that he was killed by Frank Thurrogad, a construction worker who was doing some jobs in Jones' property. He was the last person to see Jones alive. Was there a fight over money? Did he confess the killing to a friend? Did police botched the entire investigation?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mysterious Drowning in Swimming Pool
podcast.body: Brian Jones, a member of The Rolling Stones, was found dead at the bottom of his swimming pool around midnight on July 2/3, 1969. Although he still had a pulse when pulled from the water, he was dead by the time the ambulance arrived. The official verdict was death by drowning, but lingering doubts and theories persist. "One time around midnight July 2nd July 3rd 1969, Jones was found dead at the bottom of his swimming pool. When he was fished out, he still had a pulse. But by the time the ambulance arrived, he was dead."

xref.body: In late 1963, a very young Rolling Stones wrote a jingle for Rice Krispies. Brian Jones composed the music, and Mick Jagger performed the vocals. "Brian Jones wrote the music and Mick Jagger sang it."

xref.title: Rice Krispies Jingle (c. 1963-1964)
xref.body: Very early in their career, around 1963 or 1964, The Rolling Stones were commissioned to write a jingle for Rice Krispies cereal. Brian Jones was responsible for writing the music, while Mick Jagger performed the vocals for the advertisement. "Brian Jones wrote the music and Mick Jagger saying this."

xref.title: Influence on British Rock Legends
xref.body: During her European tour in the spring of 1964, Sister Rosetta Tharpe performed in Manchester, where her inspiring performance deeply affected audience members Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck, Keith Richards, and Brian Jones of The Rolling Stones. These future rock icons became her "disciples" after witnessing her groundbreaking show. "Her performance was so inspiring that it changed the lives of four notable members of the audience."
